newsitem.title: UK: British MPs quizzed on Sinn Fein parliament visit.
newsitem.headline: British MPs quizzed on Sinn Fein parliament visit.

text.p: Britain's MI5 security service has complained to the opposition Labour Party that some of its legislators recently left a leading member of the IRA's political wing unaccompanied in the British parliament.
The Party's Home Affairs spokesman, Jack Straw, said on Thursday the complaint had been taken "very seriously indeed" by the party's senior parliamentary business manager, Donald Dewar.
According to a report in the Independent newspaper, the visitor involved was suspected by MI5 of being a member of the Irish Republican Army's ruling army council.
It said this person, whom it did not name, had claimed to be going to the lavatory, and had then disappeared for 20 minutes.
But Ken Livingstone, one of the MPs who invited the Sinn Fein delegation to parliament, on Thursday poured scorn on the idea that any of the visitors were senior IRA officials.

"The idea that the IRA army council members would come to London actually to case the joint for bombing runs...these are the most wanted people in Britain, they would not risk them on that sort of exercise," he added.

Livingstone told BBC radio Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin was accompanied on the visit by two party officials. One ran its London office and the other was its expert on British government policy.

Livingstone said the three were met in the Central Lobby, where Britons go to meet their MPs, and taken to a cafeteria. "These are places that virtually anybody can get into," said Livingstone, who has long been a supporter of a united Ireland.

Livingstone said the IRA, a guerrilla organisation fighting to end British rule over Northern Ireland, was debating whether to resume the ceasefire it broke off in February. The MPs meeting the delegation had all stressed the case for doing so.
Straw, also interviewed on BBC radio, said the complaint was not that the MPs had met people connected with the IRA.
He noted that over the years, the British government itself had been in "very regular direct contact" with Sinn Fein.

But he added: "It is a breach of the (parliamentary) rules to leave guests unattended, whichever organisation they have come from, but obviously there are greater concerns about that if they do come from an organisation like Sinn Fein or the IRA.
"That is why, I understand, a complaint was made, and I know it is something that Donald Dewar took very seriously indeed," he said.
